# Optional analysis layers

These techniques are inspired by ALF's system-explorer analysis pipeline.
They are a menu, not six mandatory gates for every feature.

## 1. Static structure

- Identify languages/framework versions from manifests and lockfiles.
- Locate entry points, public APIs, module boundaries and representative implementations.
- Trace imports and actual references; regex matches are not a complete dependency graph in systems with dynamic imports, reflection or generated bindings.
- Report cycles with their actual edge chain. Label complexity/LOC proxies as estimates and state exclusions. Large files alone do not prove a design defect.

## 2. Behavioral/history analysis

- Bound history to the relevant paths and an explicit period, normally up to 12 months for a comprehensive assessment. Use read-only Git commands without external diff/textconv helpers.
- Identify change frequency, co-change and ownership evidence where relevant. Explain merge/rename handling and whether counts are measured or approximated.
- A high complexity × change-frequency proxy can prioritize a deep dive, not establish a bug. A single author does not by itself establish actual bus factor. Old code may be stable rather than abandoned.

## 3. Architecture and behavior recovery

- Treat directory grouping as an initial hypothesis; validate with dependencies, call sites and deployment units.
- Trace a few relevant journeys from input through processing, persistence/external calls, failures and response.
- Identify trust boundaries, transaction boundaries, synchronous/async interfaces and runtime ownership.
- Use Mermaid C4/flow/sequence diagrams only when helpful or requested. Do not force a layered or hexagonal architecture onto naming conventions.

## 4. Decision recovery

- Prefer ADRs, explicit documentation, relevant commit bodies, and actually read PR/issue discussions.
- Record context, decision, evidenced alternatives, consequences, sources and confidence. Separate historical rationale from your present-day recommendation.
- A dependency establishes usage, not why it was selected. Mark unsupported rationale unknown; do not turn plausible guesses into documented decisions.

## 5. Test quality

- Read test runner configuration and representative tests; identify observable assertions, error paths, fixtures, doubles and integration boundaries.
- Read existing coverage or mutation reports with their tool/version/date. Do not claim measured coverage from counting files or assertions.
- Assertion density, mock ratios and test/code size are weak heuristics, not pass/fail quality criteria. Smoke tests and property-based tests may not contain conventional assertions at every site.
- Check whether a test would fail for the behavior it claims to protect. Execution requires the caller's authority and approval for material side effects.

## 6. Infrastructure and operability

- Read CI/CD, packaging/deployment definitions, service boundaries, configuration patterns and secret references without printing secret values.
- Identify build/test commands, platform/host assumptions, version pinning, rollout/rollback, health checks and observability.
- Distinguish repository intent from confirmed live state. Do not interrogate production, start services, install tools, or apply infrastructure without explicit authorization.

## Handback

Provide scope, the relevant structure/flow, key evidence, constraints for the
caller, findings, unknowns and checks not performed. For comprehensive JSON,
use null for unknown metrics and include methodology/provenance rather than
an unexplained aggregate score.
